claims.text: The initial material is a homogeneous, uniformly dispersed mixture of Pt, Pd, Au, Ag, and Ru precursors that is not yet alloyed at the atomic level.
Heating above 10^3 K/s to approximately 923 K with a sub-second dwell sharply limits the time available for atomic diffusion.
Limited diffusion time forces near-simultaneous, stochastic co-nucleation of Pt, Pd, Au, Ag, and Ru.
Near-simultaneous co-nucleation produces a homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The ultrafast protocol produces nanoscale nuclei with frozen-in atomic configurations because atomic mobilization during nucleation is drastically reduced.
Immediate quenching arrests post-nucleation atomic diffusion.
Arresting post-nucleation diffusion prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
Preventing phase separation and segregation stabilizes uniformly alloyed nanoparticles.
Ultrafast processing will yield a more homogeneous elemental distribution than a conventional slow thermal ramp.
Ultrafast processing will yield a more consistently single-phase alloy structure than a conventional slow thermal ramp.
Ultrafast processing will increase the exposed surface area of catalytically active sites relative to slow-ramp processing.
A conventional slow thermal ramp permits enough atomic diffusion to promote elemental segregation, phase separation, or decomposition.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle systems containing at least five metal precursors in a single-source formulation.
The mechanism may not apply when other kinetic inhibitors dominate.
Insufficient control of rapid quenching can cause defect formation or incomplete alloying.
Variations in precursor chemistry, reactor design, and cooling-rate uniformity can make the outcome system-dependent.
The comparison holds precursor composition and other synthesis conditions constant while changing the thermal protocol.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in elemental homogeneity, phase purity, and surface area under ultrafast processing would falsify the proposed reduced-mobility mechanism.
